category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 1 — HAVE TO VS MUST | ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Both have to and must express obligation, duty, or necessity. The key difference is: 'have to' represents an external obligation (e.g., your boss, company, or law), while 'must' represents an internal or personal obligation (e.g., a self-imposed duty or conscious decision). For laws and instructions, we mostly use 'have to'.
exampleText: I have to complete this presentation for tomorrow's meeting.
speechPrompt: I must buy fresh vegetables and cook a healthy meal tonight.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 2 — USE OF 'HAVE TO' AND 'MUST' IN ENGLISH GRAMMAR
explanation: Must and have to express an obligation or responsibility. In negative sentences, 'must not' (mustn't) means it is prohibited, while 'don't have to' means it is not necessary. Note that 'must' has no past or future form; we use 'had to' for the past and 'will have to' for the future.
exampleText: You have to wear a seat belt when you drive.
speechPrompt: You must not leave your homework incomplete.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 3 — ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON - DIFFERENCE BETWEEN HAVE TO, OUGHT TO & SUPPOSED TO
explanation: 'Have to' or 'must' means you have no choice. 'Supposed to' indicates an obligation or a rule that you are expected to follow, but you still have a choice. 'Ought to' is used for advice or suggestions and is not as strong as 'have to' or 'supposed to'.
exampleText: I have to submit the reports tomorrow.
speechPrompt: We are supposed to submit the reports by tomorrow.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 4 — DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ‘HAVE TO’, SUPPOSE TO & OUGHT TO
explanation: Both 'have to' and 'must' express obligation, whereas 'supposed to' means an expected behavior or rule. 'Ought to' is used for suggestions and moral duties where you have a choice. In negative sentences and questions, 'ought to' is rarely used.
exampleText: I have to pay my taxes.
speechPrompt: You are not supposed to talk loudly in a hospital.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 5 — ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON - USING ‘MUST’ CORRECTLY IN SENTENCES AND QUESTIONS.
explanation: Must is a modal auxiliary verb and always takes the base form of the verb. It can express personal obligation ('I must study'), logical certainty ('This must be the right address'), or a strong recommendation ('You must visit that new place'). In questions, we often prefer 'Do you have to?' instead of 'Must you?'.
exampleText: I must finish the work before I leave.
speechPrompt: Being confident in an interview is a must.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 6 — USING ‘MUSTN'T’ AND ‘NEEDN'T’ CORRECTLY
explanation: 'Mustn't' means you are not allowed to do something (prohibition/restriction), whereas 'needn't' means it is not necessary to do something (you have a choice, it's optional).
exampleText: You mustn't tell anyone our secret.
speechPrompt: You needn't carry the documents with you today.

category: Modal Verbs — Have To / Must / Ought To / Supposed To / Need (Obligation & Necessity)
title: Lesson 7 — USING 'NEED' CORRECTLY
explanation: 'Need' can act as a main verb (meaning 'require' or 'necessity') and takes the regular verb forms ('needs to', 'needed to'). It can also act as an auxiliary verb in negative sentences ('need not') and questions ('Need we wait?').
exampleText: She needs to talk to him right now.
speechPrompt: You needn't have lost your temper.

title: Lesson 8 — ALL USES OF SHOULD IN ENGLISH | MASTER MODAL VERBS
explanation: 'Should' is used to give advice/recommendations ('You should see a doctor'), express moral duty/obligation ('You should keep promises'), or express expectations ('The package should arrive tomorrow'). 'Should have' is used for past regrets or criticism.
exampleText: You should see a doctor about that cough.
speechPrompt: I should have studied harder for the exam.

title: Lesson 9 — ALL USES OF 'SHOULD' IN ENGLISH | FUNCTIONAL ENGLISH GRAMMAR
explanation: 'Should' is a modal verb that does not change with subject ('I should', 'He should'). It is used to suggest actions or predict likely outcomes based on facts or patterns.
exampleText: Everyone should wear seatbelts in the car.
speechPrompt: I don't think you should spend your salary online.

title: Lesson 10 — USING ' SHOULD ' IN DIFFERENT WAYS - ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'should' for advising, recommendations, or predicting probabilities. In negative sentences, 'shouldn't' is used to advise against something. Use 'should have' with past participle to express regret.
exampleText: He should reach here any minute.
speechPrompt: I shouldn't have shouted at you yesterday.

category: Modal Verbs — Can / Could (Ability, Possibility & Polite Requests)
title: Lesson 11 — MASTER ALL USES OF THE MODAL VERB 'COULD' | ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: 'Could' is the past form of 'can' but can also express present possibility or polite requests. We use 'could have' for past possibilities or missed opportunities.
exampleText: Could you please help me with this project?
speechPrompt: I could have won the race, but I gave up.

category: Modal Verbs — Can / Could (Ability, Possibility & Polite Requests)
title: Lesson 12 — ALL USES OF ‘COULD’ IN PRESENT, PAST & FUTURE TENSES
explanation: 'Could' is used for past abilities ('I could swim'), future possibilities ('It could rain'), and polite requests. Do not use 'could' for specific one-time past achievements; use 'was able to' instead.
exampleText: We could go on a trip if we didn't have to work.
speechPrompt: Yesterday I couldn't lift the sofa by myself.

category: Modal Verbs — Can / Could (Ability, Possibility & Polite Requests)
title: Lesson 13 — MODAL VERBS - CAN AND COULD - ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: 'Can' is used for present ability or informal requests and permission. 'Could' is used for past ability or formal/polite requests. Always follow both with the base form of the verb.
exampleText: He can swim very well in the pool.
speechPrompt: Could I borrow your book for a day, please?

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 14 — DIFFERENCE BETWEEN WILL VS WOULD | ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'will' for real, definite, or promised future situations with high certainty. Use 'would' for imaginary, hypothetical, polite, or past habits/refusals.
exampleText: I will pick you up at six o'clock sharp.
speechPrompt: I would pick you up if I had a car.

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 15 — ALL USES OF THE MODAL VERB 'WOULD' - FUNCTIONAL ENGLISH GRAMMAR
explanation: 'Would' is a versatile modal verb used for conditionals ('If I won, I would buy a car'), future-in-the-past ('They said they would come'), past habits ('Every morning she would run'), and polite requests ('Would you mind?').
exampleText: If I had more time, I would study harder.
speechPrompt: Would you mind passing me the salt, please?

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 16 — ALL USES OF MODAL VERB 'WOULD' | ENGLISH GRAMMAR PRACTICE
explanation: 'Would' adds politeness and diplomacy in questions and statements. It contracts to 'I'd' for subjects and can express preferences like 'would rather'.
exampleText: They said they would come to the party.
speechPrompt: I'd rather take a cab than walk to the office.

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 17 — 'WILL I/WE' OR 'SHALL I/WE' IN QUESTIONS (FUTURE) - WHICH ONE IS CORRECT?
explanation: Use 'shall I/we' when offering to do something or initiating an action. Use 'will I/we' when asking about future outcomes where you are not offering or controlling the action.
exampleText: Shall we wait for you at the library?
speechPrompt: Will I recover soon from this cold, doctor?

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 18 — USING THE AUXILIARY VERB - WOULD - FREE ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'would' for past habits, indirect speech 'will' conversion, conditional sentences, or expressing preferences with 'would rather'.
exampleText: I would read a lot in my college days.
speechPrompt: Would you mind helping me with my project?

category: Modal Verbs — Will / Would / Shall (Intentions, Habits & Future)
title: Lesson 19 — USING 'WILL' - GRAMMAR ESL LESSON
explanation: Use 'will' to talk about certain future events, beliefs with words like 'probably/maybe', decisions made at the moment of speaking, or promises.
exampleText: The sun will rise over there tomorrow.
speechPrompt: Perhaps we will meet again someday.

title: Lesson 20 — USING MAY AND MIGHT - BASIC ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'may' for formal permissions ('May I leave?') and higher possibilities. Use 'might' for smaller or less likely possibilities.
exampleText: He may come to stay with us next week.
speechPrompt: I might have forgotten my keys at the cafe.

category: Past Modal Verbs (May Have / Might Have / Must Have / Could Have / Should Have / Would Have)
title: Lesson 21 — MAY HAVE VS MIGHT HAVE VS MUST HAVE | PAST MODAL VERBS
explanation: 'May have' and 'might have' show around 50% or less certainty about a past event. 'Must have' shows high logical certainty based on strong evidence or facts.
exampleText: She may have gone to the library.
speechPrompt: He must have left his phone at home.

category: Past Modal Verbs (May Have / Might Have / Must Have / Could Have / Should Have / Would Have)
title: Lesson 22 — MODAL VERBS OF THE PAST – MAY HAVE, MIGHT HAVE, MUST HAVE — WHAT’S THE DIFFERENCE?
explanation: 'May have' is more formal; 'might have' is more common in spoken English. 'Must have' expresses an educated guess based on logic or results.
exampleText: We may have taken the wrong road.
speechPrompt: She must have been crying; her eyes are red.

category: Past Modal Verbs (May Have / Might Have / Must Have / Could Have / Should Have / Would Have)
title: Lesson 23 — PAST MODAL VERBS – COULD HAVE, SHOULD HAVE, WOULD HAVE, MIGHT HAVE, MUST HAVE
explanation: Past modal verbs use 'modal + have + past participle'. 'Could have' is missed possibility; 'should have' is past regret; 'would have' is imaginary past outcome.
exampleText: I could have completed my graduation, but I didn't.
speechPrompt: I should have studied harder for the exam.

category: Past Modal Verbs (May Have / Might Have / Must Have / Could Have / Should Have / Would Have)
title: Lesson 24 — USING SHOULD, COULD AND WOULD HAVE DONE CORRECTLY
explanation: 'Should have done' implies a missed obligation or regret. 'Could have done' means a choice or possibility you decided not to take. 'Would have done' means you wanted to but were stopped by circumstances.
exampleText: You should have been more careful.
speechPrompt: I would have completed my project, but there was no electricity.

title: Lesson 25 — ALL USES OF BEEN AND BEING | FUNCTIONAL ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: 'Been' is the past participle of be, used with has/have/had. 'Being' is the present participle, used with am/is/are/was/were for temporary behaviors or passive continuous tenses.
exampleText: I have been to London twice.
speechPrompt: You are being rude to her right now.

title: Lesson 26 — MASTER ALL USES OF BEING
explanation: 'Being' can express temporary behavior, passive voice ('The car is being washed'), temporary emotional state, or act as a gerund/noun ('I love being a teacher').
exampleText: The road is being repaired at the moment.
speechPrompt: Thank you for being so patient with us.

title: Lesson 27 — MASTER ALL USES OF BEEN
explanation: 'Been' has eight main uses, including travel/experiences ('I've been to Japan'), states/conditions, ongoing actions, visits, and passive perfect voice.
exampleText: We have been studying for hours.
speechPrompt: I've been busy with work all week.

title: Lesson 28 — HOW TO USE BEING IN ENGLISH? – ENGLISH GRAMMAR LESSON
explanation: Use 'being' for temporary action or behavior followed by an adjective, in passive voice, or as a replacement for 'since', 'as', or 'because'. Do not use 'being' to show simple emotions like 'I was being upset'.
exampleText: Why are you being so silly?
speechPrompt: Being a friend of the actor, I am invited to parties.

title: Lesson 29 — WHEN TO USE HAVE & HAVING? GRAMMAR DOUBT SOLVED!
explanation: Use 'have' for permanent possession, relationships, or state. Use 'having' for ongoing temporary actions like meals, events, or short experiences.
exampleText: I have a laptop and a car.
speechPrompt: We are having a meeting at the office.

title: Lesson 30 — WHEN TO USE HAD HAD IN ONE SENTENCE? ​​ PAST PERFECT TENSE MADE SIMPLE
explanation: 'Had had' is correct in the past perfect tense. The first 'had' is the auxiliary verb; the second 'had' is the past participle meaning experienced, possessed, or eaten.
exampleText: I had had breakfast before I left for work.
speechPrompt: She had had a headache before she took medicine.

title: Lesson 31 — HOW TO USE ‘HAVE HAD’ CORRECTLY IN ONE SENTENCE?
explanation: 'Have had' is the present perfect tense of 'have'. Use it to show continuous possession from past to present, or completed actions within a current time frame.
exampleText: We have had this car for four years.
speechPrompt: She has had a headache since yesterday.

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 32 — Auxiliary Verbs: 'Do' and 'Does' in Questions & Negatives
explanation: Use 'do' with I, you, we, they and 'does' with he, she, it to form present simple questions and negative statements. Remember that after 'does' or 'doesn't', the main verb returns to its base form (e.g., 'Does she like...?' not 'likes').
exampleText: Does she speak English fluently at work?
speechPrompt: Do you prefer tea or coffee in the morning?

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 33 — Auxiliary Verb 'Did' in Past Simple Tense
explanation: Use 'did' for all subjects (I, you, he, she, we, they) when forming questions or negatives in the past simple. Once 'did' or 'didn't' is used, the main verb stays in its base form.
exampleText: Did you complete the project report yesterday?
speechPrompt: I didn't hear the phone ring during the meeting.

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 34 — Auxiliary 'Have' & 'Has' in Present Perfect Sentences
explanation: Use 'have' (I, you, we, they) or 'has' (he, she, it) combined with the past participle (V3) to form the present perfect tense, describing actions with present relevance.
exampleText: She has lived in London for five years.
speechPrompt: We have finished all our assignments for this week.

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 35 — Auxiliary 'Be' (Am/Is/Are/Was/Were) in Continuous Tenses
explanation: The auxiliary verb 'be' combines with present participles (-ing) to create continuous tenses, showing ongoing actions in the present or past.
exampleText: They were discussing the new budget when I entered.
speechPrompt: I am currently preparing for my English fluency test.

category: Auxiliary Verbs — Do / Does / Did / Have / Has / Be
title: Lesson 36 — Emphatic 'Do', 'Does', and 'Did' for Strong Assertions
explanation: You can place 'do', 'does', or 'did' before a main verb in affirmative sentences to add strong emphasis or contrast a previous doubt (e.g., 'I do care about your progress').
exampleText: I do appreciate all the support you have given me.
speechPrompt: She does know how to solve this difficult problem.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 37 — Present Perfect Simple: Life Experiences & Recent Actions
explanation: Present Perfect Simple connects past events with the present moment. Use it for life experiences ('I have visited Japan'), accomplishments, or recent events without specifying an exact past time.
exampleText: I have already seen that movie twice.
speechPrompt: Have you ever traveled abroad on your own?

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 38 — Present Perfect Continuous: Ongoing Unfinished Actions
explanation: Formed with 'have/has been + verb-ing', this tense emphasizes the duration or ongoing nature of an action that started in the past and continues into the present.
exampleText: She has been studying English for three hours.
speechPrompt: It has been raining continuously since morning.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 39 — Present Perfect Simple vs Present Perfect Continuous
explanation: Use Present Perfect Simple when focusing on completion, result, or quantity ('I have written three letters'). Use Present Perfect Continuous when focusing on duration, process, or activity ('I have been writing all morning').
exampleText: He has been painting the room all day, and he has painted two walls so far.
speechPrompt: I have been calling him, but he hasn't answered yet.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 40 — Past Perfect Simple ('Had Done') for Earlier Past Actions
explanation: Past Perfect Simple ('had + V3') indicates an action that happened before another past event or a specific point in the past.
exampleText: When I arrived at the station, the train had already left.
speechPrompt: She had finished her work before the manager asked for it.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 41 — Past Perfect Continuous ('Had Been Doing')
explanation: Use 'had been + verb-ing' to describe an ongoing action that was taking place up until another moment in the past, emphasizing duration.
exampleText: They had been waiting for over an hour before the bus finally arrived.
speechPrompt: I had been working there for five years when the company closed.
optionsString: had been waiting,were waiting,have been waiting,waited

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 42 — Future Perfect Simple ('Will Have Done')
explanation: Use 'will have + past participle' to state that an action will be completed before a specified time in the future.
exampleText: By next month, I will have completed my degree.
speechPrompt: They will have finished the building by December.

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 43 — Future Perfect Continuous ('Will Have Been Doing')
explanation: Use 'will have been + verb-ing' to project into the future and express the duration of an ongoing action up to a given future point.
exampleText: By 5 PM, she will have been working for eight hours straight.
speechPrompt: Next year, we will have been living here for a decade.
optionsString: will have been working,will work,is working,will be working

category: Perfect Tenses (Present, Past & Future Perfect / Perfect Continuous)
title: Lesson 44 — Master Perfect Tenses in Conversational Fluency
explanation: Mastering perfect tenses allows you to tell stories with accurate time sequencing and express subtle relationships between past, present, and future events.
exampleText: I had been hoping to meet her, but she had already left.
speechPrompt: How long have you been practicing English today?
optionsString: have you been,had you been,were you,are you

title: Lesson 45 — Simple Present Tense: Habits, Routines & Universal Truths
explanation: Use simple present for regular habits, daily routines, facts, and permanent situations. Add '-s' or '-es' for third-person singular subjects (he, she, it).
exampleText: The sun rises in the east every morning.
speechPrompt: He plays tennis every Saturday morning with his friends.

title: Lesson 46 — Present Continuous Tense: Actions Happening Right Now
explanation: Use 'am/is/are + verb-ing' to describe actions taking place at the exact moment of speaking or temporary situations occurring around now.
exampleText: Please be quiet; the baby is sleeping.
speechPrompt: I am reading an interesting book on psychology.

title: Lesson 47 — Simple Past Tense: Completed Past Actions & Dates
explanation: Use simple past to describe finished actions that occurred at a specific time in the past. Regular verbs take '-ed', while irregular verbs change form (e.g., go -> went).
exampleText: We visited our grandparents last weekend.
speechPrompt: I bought a new laptop yesterday afternoon.

title: Lesson 48 — Past Continuous Tense: Ongoing Background Past Actions
explanation: Use 'was/were + verb-ing' to set a scene or describe an action that was in progress at a specific time in the past.
exampleText: At 8 PM yesterday, I was watching a documentary.
speechPrompt: They were playing football when it started to rain.

title: Lesson 49 — Simple Past vs Past Continuous: Interrupted Actions
explanation: Combine Past Continuous (background long action) and Simple Past (short interrupting action) using 'when' or 'while' (e.g., 'While I was cooking, the doorbell rang').
exampleText: I was sleeping when the alarm rang.
speechPrompt: While she was driving to work, she saw a magnificent rainbow.

title: Lesson 50 — Stative Verbs: Why Certain Verbs Don't Take '-ing'
explanation: Stative verbs describe states of mind, emotions, senses, and possession (e.g., love, know, want, belong, understand). They are normally used in simple tenses, not continuous forms.
exampleText: I understand the grammar rule clearly now.
speechPrompt: She knows the answer to that tricky question.

title: Lesson 51 — Dynamic vs Stative Uses of Verbs (Think, Have, See)
explanation: Some verbs can be both stative and dynamic depending on meaning. For example, 'I think you are right' (opinion - stative) vs 'I am thinking about the offer' (mental activity - dynamic).
exampleText: I am thinking about moving to a new city.
speechPrompt: I think this is a fantastic opportunity for all of us.

title: Lesson 52 — Expressing Future: 'Will' vs 'Going To' vs Present Continuous
explanation: Use 'will' for spontaneous decisions or predictions based on opinion. Use 'be going to' for prior plans or evidence-based predictions. Use Present Continuous for fixed arrangements.
exampleText: I am meeting the doctor tomorrow at 10 AM.
speechPrompt: Look at those dark clouds; it is going to rain soon.

title: Lesson 53 — Future Time Clauses: Present Simple After 'When', 'If', 'As Soon As'
explanation: In future time clauses introduced by conjunctions like when, as soon as, before, after, or if, use the Present Simple tense to refer to future time.
exampleText: I will call you as soon as I arrive at the hotel.
speechPrompt: When he comes home, we will start dinner immediately.

category: Questions & Question Formation (incl. Tag Questions & Wh-Questions)
title: Lesson 54 — Wh- Question Formation: Word Order Rules
explanation: Standard question structure: Wh- Word + Auxiliary Verb + Subject + Main Verb (e.g., 'Where do you live?'). Ensure the auxiliary verb matches the tense and subject.
exampleText: Where did you buy that beautiful jacket?
speechPrompt: What time does the morning train depart?
optionsString: you bought,did you buy,bought you,do you bought

category: Questions & Question Formation (incl. Tag Questions & Wh-Questions)
title: Lesson 55 — Subject Questions vs Object Questions
explanation: If the question word asks about the subject, do not use auxiliary verbs 'do/does/did' (e.g., 'Who broke the vase?'). If it asks about the object, use auxiliary verbs (e.g., 'Who did you call?').
exampleText: Who called you late last night?
speechPrompt: Who gave you this wonderful advice?
optionsString: Who called,Who did call,Who calling,Who was called

category: Questions & Question Formation (incl. Tag Questions & Wh-Questions)
title: Lesson 56 — Question Tags: Positive/Negative Matching Rules
explanation: Question tags confirm information. A positive statement takes a negative tag ('You live here, don't you?'), and a negative statement takes a positive tag ('You aren't tired, are you?').
exampleText: She is coming to the party tonight, isn't she?
speechPrompt: You haven't seen my car keys, have you?

category: Questions & Question Formation (incl. Tag Questions & Wh-Questions)
title: Lesson 57 — Indirect Questions for Polite Conversation
explanation: Indirect questions sound polite (e.g., 'Could you tell me where the bank is?'). Notice that in indirect questions, the word order changes back to normal statement order (subject before verb).
exampleText: Do you know where the nearest post office is?
speechPrompt: I was wondering if you could help me with this task.
optionsString: where is the bank,where the bank is,the bank where is,is where the bank

title: Lesson 58 — Zero & First Conditionals: Facts & Real Possibilities
explanation: Zero conditional (If + Present Simple, Present Simple) states general scientific facts ('If water boils, it turns to steam'). First conditional (If + Present Simple, Will + Verb) expresses real future possibilities.
exampleText: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
speechPrompt: If you study consistently, you will improve your English skills.

title: Lesson 59 — Second Conditional: Hypothetical Present & Advice
explanation: Use Second Conditional (If + Past Simple, Would + Base Verb) for hypothetical or imaginary present situations. Use 'If I were you...' to give friendly advice.
exampleText: If I had a million dollars, I would buy a house on the coast.
speechPrompt: If I were you, I would take that job offer immediately.

title: Lesson 60 — Third Conditional: Unreal Past & Regrets
explanation: Use Third Conditional (If + Past Perfect, Would Have + V3) to talk about imaginary past events that did not happen and express regret or relief.
exampleText: If I had set my alarm, I would not have missed the bus.
speechPrompt: If we had left earlier, we would have avoided the traffic jams.

title: Lesson 61 — Coordinating Conjunctions: FANBOYS Rules
explanation: Coordinating conjunctions (For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So) join equal clauses or words. Always place a comma before them when connecting independent clauses.
exampleText: Example: I wanted to go for a walk, but it began to rain.
speechPrompt: He was exhausted, yet he continued running.

title: Lesson 62 — Subordinating Conjunctions: Reason & Cause
explanation: Use subordinating conjunctions like because, since, as, and due to the fact that to introduce clauses explaining reasons.
exampleText: Example: Since it was holiday, the offices were closed.
speechPrompt: We stayed inside because the weather was stormy.

title: Lesson 63 — Correlative Conjunctions: Pairs in Harmony
explanation: Correlative conjunctions work in pairs (both...and, either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also). Ensure parallel grammatical structures after each part.
exampleText: Example: Not only did he win the prize, but he also set a new record.
speechPrompt: You can either choose the red coat or the blue jacket.

title: Lesson 64 — Conjunctions of Contrast: Although vs Despite
explanation: Although, even though, and though take a full clause (subject + verb). Despite and in spite of take a noun phrase or gerund (-ing).
exampleText: Example: Although it was cold, we went swimming.
speechPrompt: Despite the heavy rain, they arrived on time.

title: Lesson 65 — Conjunctions of Purpose & Result: So That & In Order To
explanation: Use 'so that + clause' or 'in order to + verb' to express purpose and intention clearly.
exampleText: Example: She saved money so that she could buy a car.
speechPrompt: He woke up early in order to catch the first train.

title: Lesson 66 — Sentence Connectors: However, Furthermore, Therefore
explanation: Transition words connect ideas between separate sentences. Place a semicolon or period before them and a comma immediately after.
exampleText: Example: The exam was difficult; however, most students passed.
speechPrompt: She is very talented; furthermore, she works extremely hard.

title: Lesson 67 — Mastering Conjunctions for Cohesive Speech
explanation: Connecting thoughts smoothly with appropriate conjunctions eliminates choppy sentences and boosts spoken fluency.
exampleText: Example: I enjoy reading books, whereas my brother prefers watching movies.
speechPrompt: Although I was tired, I finished my work before midnight.

title: Lesson 68 — Prepositions of Time: In, On, At Detailed Rules
explanation: Use 'at' for specific times/moments (at 5 PM, at noon), 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on May 1st), and 'in' for longer periods (in July, in 2024, in the morning).
exampleText: Example: The train leaves at 9:30 AM on Tuesday.
speechPrompt: My birthday is in September.

title: Lesson 69 — Prepositions of Place: In, On, At Spatial Concepts
explanation: Use 'at' for specific points or locations (at the door), 'on' for surfaces (on the table), and 'in' for enclosed spaces or areas (in the room, in London).
exampleText: Example: She is sitting at her desk in the main office.
speechPrompt: There is a beautiful painting on the wall.

title: Lesson 70 — Prepositions of Movement: Into, Onto, Through, Across
explanation: Prepositions of movement describe direction. 'Into' means entering an enclosed space; 'onto' means moving to a surface; 'through' means passing inside a 3D space.
exampleText: Example: He walked into the building and went up the stairs.
speechPrompt: The boat sailed across the calm river.

title: Lesson 71 — Dependent Prepositions with Popular Adjectives
explanation: Many adjectives are paired with specific prepositions (e.g., interested in, good at, famous for, afraid of, allergic to). Memorize these fixed pairs.
exampleText: Example: She is exceptionally good at solving complex math puzzles.
speechPrompt: He is deeply interested in learning ancient history.

title: Lesson 72 — Dependent Prepositions with Common Verbs
explanation: Verbs often take specific prepositions (e.g., depend on, belong to, listen to, suffer from, apology for).
exampleText: Example: Success depends on your dedication and effort.
speechPrompt: Who does this briefcase belong to?

title: Lesson 73 — Prepositional Phrases with 'In': Fixed Idiomatic Uses
explanation: Phrases like 'in detail', 'in advance', 'in fact', 'in public', and 'in brief' are set expressions in spoken and written English.
exampleText: Example: Please let us know your decision in advance.
speechPrompt: In fact, she had already solved the problem.

title: Lesson 74 — Prepositional Phrases with 'At': Common Expressions
explanation: Master fixed phrases like 'at last', 'at least', 'at present', 'at first glance', and 'at risk'.
exampleText: Example: At last, the rainy weather cleared up.
speechPrompt: You should spend at least thirty minutes reading daily.

title: Lesson 75 — Prepositional Phrases with 'On': On Time vs On Purpose
explanation: Phrases like 'on time' (punctual), 'on purpose' (intentionally), 'on duty', and 'on average' add precision to your speech.
exampleText: Example: He showed up right on time for the meeting.
speechPrompt: I am certain he didn't break the vase on purpose.

title: Lesson 76 — Prepositional Phrases with 'By': Transportation & Accident
explanation: Use 'by' for modes of transit (by bus, by train, by air) and accidental causes (by chance, by mistake). Note: 'on foot' is an exception.
exampleText: Example: I grabbed his umbrella by mistake.
speechPrompt: They traveled across Europe by train.

title: Lesson 77 — Prepositions 'Under' & 'Over' in Idiomatic Phrases
explanation: Phrases like 'under pressure', 'under construction', 'over time', and 'over the weekend' describe continuous conditions.
exampleText: Example: She works exceptionally well under pressure.
speechPrompt: Road repairs will be completed over the weekend.

title: Lesson 78 — Differences: 'In the end' vs 'At the end'
explanation: 'At the end' refers to the final point of something tangible (at the end of the road/movie). 'In the end' means 'finally' or 'eventually' after a process.
exampleText: Example: In the end, everything worked out perfectly.
speechPrompt: There is a summary at the end of each chapter.
optionsString: In the end,At the end,To the end,By the end

title: Lesson 79 — Differences: 'On time' vs 'In time'
explanation: 'On time' means punctual according to a schedule. 'In time' means early enough before a deadline or event.
exampleText: Example: The flight landed right on time.
speechPrompt: We arrived in time to see the opening ceremony.

title: Lesson 80 — Prepositions Following Nouns (Reason for, Solution to)
explanation: Nouns take specific prepositions: reason for, solution to, advantage of, relationship with, impact on.
exampleText: Example: What was the main reason for the sudden delay?
speechPrompt: Scientists are working on a solution to climate change.

title: Lesson 81 — Prepositions of Cause & Reason: Due To vs Because Of
explanation: 'Because of' is followed by a noun phrase. 'Due to' functions similarly but often follows a link verb like 'is' or 'was'.
exampleText: Example: The match was canceled because of heavy rainfall.
speechPrompt: His late arrival was due to severe traffic.

title: Lesson 82 — Prepositions with Means of Transport & Vehicles
explanation: Use 'in' for private vehicles (in a car, in a taxi). Use 'on' for public or large transport (on a bus, on a plane, on a train).
exampleText: Example: I saw him sitting on the subway train this morning.
speechPrompt: We rode in my friend's car to the beach.

title: Lesson 83 — Eliminating Common Preposition Errors in Speaking
explanation: Avoid adding unnecessary prepositions after verbs like discuss ('discuss the topic', NOT 'discuss about'), enter ('enter the room'), or answer ('answer the question').
exampleText: Example: We need to discuss the project timeline today.
speechPrompt: She entered the office silently.

title: Lesson 84 — Advanced Prepositions: Besides, Except For, Apart From
explanation: 'Besides' means 'in addition to'. 'Except for' or 'apart from' means excluding or leaving out.
exampleText: Example: Besides English, she speaks Spanish and French fluently.
speechPrompt: Everyone attended the seminar except for John.

title: Lesson 85 — Prepositions in Official Phrases: According to & With Regard to
explanation: Use 'according to' when citing sources and 'with regard to' when introducing a business topic.
exampleText: Example: According to the news report, temperatures will drop tomorrow.
speechPrompt: I am writing with regard to your recent job application.
optionsString: According to,With regard to,In spite of,Due to

title: Lesson 86 — Preposition Placement in Questions & Preposition Stranding
explanation: In conversational questions, prepositions naturally fall at the end of the clause ('What are you looking at?' / 'Who did you talk to?').
exampleText: Example: What kind of music are you listening to?
speechPrompt: Who were you speaking with on the phone?

title: Lesson 87 — Borrow vs Lend vs Keep
explanation: 'Borrow' means to take temporarily ('Can I borrow your pen?'). 'Lend' means to give temporarily ('I will lend you my book'). 'Keep' means to hold permanently or long-term.
exampleText: Example: Could you lend me your umbrella until tomorrow?
speechPrompt: I borrowed a coat from my brother for the winter trip.

title: Lesson 88 — Rob vs Steal
explanation: 'Rob' focuses on the victim or place robbed ('They robbed the bank'). 'Steal' focuses on the item taken ('He stole a wallet').
exampleText: Example: Someone stole my bicycle from the driveway.
speechPrompt: The thieves robbed three local jewelry stores.

title: Lesson 89 — Study vs Learn vs Teach
explanation: 'Study' is the process of reading/practicing. 'Learn' is acquiring knowledge or skill. 'Teach' is imparting knowledge to others.
exampleText: Example: She wants to learn how to play the piano.
speechPrompt: He studies for two hours every evening.

title: Lesson 90 — Rise vs Raise vs Arise
explanation: 'Rise' is intransitive (no direct object: 'Prices rise'). 'Raise' is transitive (takes an object: 'Raise your hand'). 'Arise' means to come into notice or happen.
exampleText: Example: Please raise your hand if you have a question.
speechPrompt: The sun will rise at six in the morning.

title: Lesson 91 — Lie vs Lay vs Lain
explanation: 'Lie' means to recline or rest (intransitive: 'Lie down'). 'Lay' means to place something down (transitive: 'Lay the book on the table'). Past tense of lie is lay; past of lay is laid.
exampleText: Example: Please lay the blanket gently on the grass.
speechPrompt: I need to lie down for a short nap.

title: Lesson 92 — Say vs Tell vs Speak vs Talk
explanation: Use 'tell' with a personal object ('Tell me the story'). Use 'say' without a personal object ('Say hello'). Use 'speak/talk' for languages or general dialogue.
exampleText: Example: She told me that she was leaving early.
speechPrompt: He said that he would call us back.

title: Lesson 93 — Hear vs Listen
explanation: 'Hear' is passive perception of sound. 'Listen' is active, focused attention (requires 'to': 'Listen to the music').
exampleText: Example: Did you hear that strange noise outside?
speechPrompt: Please listen carefully to the speaker.

title: Lesson 94 — See vs Look vs Watch
explanation: 'See' is automatic visual perception. 'Look' is directing your eyes at something ('Look at this'). 'Watch' is paying attention to something moving over time.
exampleText: Example: We sat on the couch to watch a movie.
speechPrompt: Look at those colorful flowers in the garden.

title: Lesson 95 — Make vs Do
explanation: Use 'do' for actions, obligations, jobs, and repetitive tasks ('do homework, do research'). Use 'make' for creating, producing, or causing results ('make dinner, make mistakes').
exampleText: Example: I need to make an important phone call now.
speechPrompt: She does her best in every project.

title: Lesson 96 — Bring vs Take vs Fetch
explanation: 'Bring' is movement toward the speaker ('Bring it here'). 'Take' is movement away from the speaker ('Take this to him'). 'Fetch' is going, getting, and returning.
exampleText: Example: Please bring me a glass of water from the kitchen.
speechPrompt: Don't forget to take your umbrella when you leave.

title: Lesson 97 — Come vs Go
explanation: 'Come' indicates movement toward the speaker or listener's location. 'Go' indicates movement away from the current location.
exampleText: Example: Are you coming to my party tonight?
speechPrompt: We are planning to go to Spain next summer.

title: Lesson 98 — Remember vs Remind
explanation: 'Remember' is keeping or recalling memory yourself. 'Remind' is causing someone else to remember ('Remind me to call').
exampleText: Example: Please remind me to send that email before 5 PM.
speechPrompt: I distinctly remember locking the front door.

title: Lesson 99 — Advise vs Advice
explanation: 'Advise' is the verb (pronounced /ədˈvaɪz/). 'Advice' is the uncountable noun (pronounced /ədˈvaɪs/).
exampleText: Example: My doctor advised me to get more exercise.
speechPrompt: She gave me valuable advice about my career.

title: Lesson 100 — Effect vs Affect
explanation: 'Affect' is usually a verb meaning to influence. 'Effect' is usually a noun meaning a result or consequence.
exampleText: Example: The rainy weather will affect our outdoor plans.
speechPrompt: The new policy had a positive effect on sales.

title: Lesson 101 — Accept vs Except
explanation: 'Accept' is a verb meaning to receive or agree to. 'Except' is a preposition meaning excluding.
exampleText: Example: I gladly accept your invitation to the party.
speechPrompt: Everyone arrived on time except for Mark.

title: Lesson 102 — Loose vs Lose
explanation: 'Loose' is an adjective meaning not tight. 'Lose' is a verb meaning to misplace something or fail to win.
exampleText: Example: Be careful not to lose your passport.
speechPrompt: This coat is very loose on me.

title: Lesson 103 — Everyday vs Every day
explanation: 'Everyday' (one word) is an adjective meaning ordinary or daily ('everyday clothes'). 'Every day' (two words) is an adverbial phrase meaning each day.
exampleText: Example: I practice speaking English every day.
speechPrompt: Stress has become part of everyday life.

title: Lesson 104 — Then vs Than
explanation: 'Then' refers to time, sequence, or consequence ('Do this, then that'). 'Than' is used exclusively in comparisons ('He is taller than me').
exampleText: Example: She is much more experienced than I am.
speechPrompt: We ate dinner and then went for a walk.

title: Lesson 105 — Their vs There vs They're
explanation: 'Their' shows possession ('their car'). 'There' indicates place or existence ('over there'). 'They're' is the contraction for 'they are'.
exampleText: Example: They're going to present their new project over there.
speechPrompt: The students forgot their textbooks.

title: Lesson 106 — Its vs It's
explanation: 'Its' is the possessive form ('The dog wagged its tail'). 'It's' is the contraction for 'it is' or 'it has'.
exampleText: Example: It's going to be a wonderful afternoon.
speechPrompt: The company updated its privacy policy.

title: Lesson 107 — Your vs You're
explanation: 'Your' is a possessive pronoun ('your hat'). 'You're' is the contraction for 'you are'.
exampleText: Example: You're going to love this new restaurant.
speechPrompt: Is this your umbrella left on the chair?

title: Lesson 108 — Whose vs Who's
explanation: 'Whose' shows possession ('Whose phone is ringing?'). 'Who's' is the contraction for 'who is' or 'who has'.
exampleText: Example: Who's coming to the team lunch today?
speechPrompt: Whose jacket is this sitting on the bench?

title: Lesson 109 — Stationary vs Stationery
explanation: 'Stationary' means standing still or not moving. 'Stationery' refers to writing materials like paper and envelopes.
exampleText: Example: The car remained stationary at the red light.
speechPrompt: I bought new letterheads and envelopes at the stationery shop.

title: Lesson 110 — Principal vs Principle
explanation: 'Principal' means chief/main or a school head. 'Principle' refers to a fundamental rule, truth, or moral value.
exampleText: Example: Honesty is an important moral principle.
speechPrompt: Mr. Davis is the principal of our high school.

title: Lesson 111 — Beside vs Besides
explanation: 'Beside' means by the side of or next to. 'Besides' means in addition to or moreover.
exampleText: Example: She sat beside me during the conference.
speechPrompt: Besides reading, I enjoy cooking and painting.

title: Lesson 112 — Among vs Between
explanation: Use 'between' when referring to distinct, individual items (usually two). Use 'among' when referring to a group or collective body of three or more.
exampleText: Example: The prize money was divided equally among the four winners.
speechPrompt: There is a secret agreement between the two directors.

title: Lesson 113 — Sometime vs Sometimes vs Some time
explanation: 'Sometime' means at an unspecified time. 'Sometimes' means occasionally. 'Some time' means a span of time.
exampleText: Example: We should get together for coffee sometime.
speechPrompt: Sometimes I like to listen to classical music.

title: Lesson 114 — Altogether vs All together
explanation: 'Altogether' means completely or entirely. 'All together' means gathered in one place as a group.
exampleText: Example: It was an altogether enjoyable experience.
speechPrompt: We stood all together for the group photograph.

title: Lesson 115 — Compliment vs Complement
explanation: 'Compliment' means praise or admiration. 'Complement' means to complete or go well together with.
exampleText: Example: The blue shirt complements your eyes perfectly.
speechPrompt: She paid me a nice compliment on my speech.

title: Lesson 116 — Emigrate vs Immigrate
explanation: 'Emigrate' means to leave one's home country. 'Immigrate' means to move into a new country to live permanently.
exampleText: Example: They emigrated from Italy in 1995 and immigrated to Canada.
speechPrompt: My grandparents immigrated to America eighty years ago.

title: Lesson 117 — Historic vs Historical
explanation: 'Historic' means famous, important, or monumental in history. 'Historical' means related to the study or facts of history.
exampleText: Example: Signing the treaty was a historic moment.
speechPrompt: She loves reading historical novels set in the 18th century.

title: Lesson 118 — Economic vs Economical
explanation: 'Economic' relates to the economy, finance, or trade. 'Economical' means thrifty, inexpensive, or avoiding waste.
exampleText: Example: Buying energy-saving bulbs is very economical.
speechPrompt: The government announced new economic policies today.

title: Lesson 119 — Sensible vs Sensitive
explanation: 'Sensible' means reasonable, practical, or wise. 'Sensitive' means easily hurt, empathetic, or delicate.
exampleText: Example: Wearing comfortable walking shoes was a very sensible decision.
speechPrompt: She is very sensitive to loud noises and bright lights.

title: Lesson 120 — Desert vs Dessert
explanation: 'Desert' (stress on first syllable) is an arid land; as a verb, it means to abandon. 'Dessert' (stress on second syllable) is a sweet dish.
exampleText: Example: We had delicious chocolate cake for dessert.
speechPrompt: Camels can travel long distances across the desert.

title: Lesson 121 — Quiet vs Quite vs Quit
explanation: 'Quiet' means silent/peaceful. 'Quite' means fairly, completely, or very. 'Quit' means to stop or leave.
exampleText: Example: Please be quiet while the test is taking place.
speechPrompt: The news was quite unexpected and surprising.

title: Lesson 122 — Capital vs Capitol
explanation: 'Capital' refers to a chief city, uppercase letter, or financial wealth. 'Capitol' specifically refers to a building housing a legislature.
exampleText: Example: Paris is the capital of France.
speechPrompt: The senators gathered inside the Capitol building.

title: Lesson 123 — Continuous vs Continual
explanation: 'Continuous' means unbroken without any interruption. 'Continual' means occurring repeatedly over time with short breaks.
exampleText: Example: The continuous noise from the highway kept me awake.
speechPrompt: His continual interruptions disturbed the whole presentation.

title: Lesson 124 — Farther vs Further
explanation: 'Farther' refers to measurable physical distance. 'Further' refers to figurative distance, degree, or additional information.
exampleText: Example: We need to discuss this topic further before deciding.
speechPrompt: How much farther is it to the top of the hill?

title: Lesson 125 — Fewer vs Less
explanation: Use 'fewer' with plural countable nouns ('fewer books'). Use 'less' with singular uncountable nouns ('less sugar').
exampleText: Example: There were fewer people at the meeting than expected.
speechPrompt: Please add less sugar to my tea.

title: Lesson 126 — Number vs Amount
explanation: Use 'number' with countable nouns ('a number of cars'). Use 'amount' with uncountable nouns ('an amount of money').
exampleText: Example: A large number of students registered for the course.
speechPrompt: A significant amount of water was wasted.

title: Lesson 127 — Uninterested vs Disinterested
explanation: 'Uninterested' means not interested or bored. 'Disinterested' means impartial, unbiased, or neutral.
exampleText: Example: A judge must remain completely disinterested in the trial outcome.
speechPrompt: He seemed totally uninterested in the conversation.

title: Lesson 128 — Person vs People vs Persons vs Peoples
explanation: 'Person' is singular. 'People' is plural for human beings. 'Persons' is formal legal usage. 'Peoples' refers to distinct ethnic groups or nations.
exampleText: Example: Many people attended the cultural festival.
speechPrompt: She is a kind and thoughtful person.

title: Lesson 129 — Mastering Commonly Confused Words in Context
explanation: Differentiating confusing word pairs significantly elevates your accuracy and authority in spoken and written English.
exampleText: Example: Ensure you accept feedback and learn from every mistake.
speechPrompt: I need to ensure all details are correct.

title: Lesson 130 — Subject vs Object Pronouns Rules
explanation: Use subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) as the doer of the verb. Use object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) after verbs and prepositions.
exampleText: Example: She and I went to the store together.
speechPrompt: The manager gave him and me the new assignment.

title: Lesson 131 — Possessive Adjectives vs Possessive Pronouns
explanation: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, our, their) come before nouns. Possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) stand alone.
exampleText: Example: This hat is mine, and that coat is yours.
speechPrompt: Is this your notebook on the desk?

title: Lesson 132 — Reflexive & Emphatic Pronouns (Myself, Yourself)
explanation: Use reflexive pronouns when the subject and object are the same person ('I hurt myself'). Use emphatic pronouns to add emphasis ('I completed it myself').
exampleText: Example: I prepared the entire presentation myself.
speechPrompt: She looked at herself in the mirror.

title: Lesson 133 — Relative Pronouns: Who, Whom, Whose, Which, That
explanation: Use 'who' for people (subject), 'whom' for people (object), 'whose' for possession, 'which' for things, and 'that' for essential clauses.
exampleText: Example: The doctor who treated me was extremely kind.
speechPrompt: This is the camera that I bought last week.

title: Lesson 134 — Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clauses
explanation: Defining clauses provide essential information (no commas). Non-defining clauses add extra details (separated by commas, 'which' or 'who', never 'that').
exampleText: Example: My brother, who lives in Chicago, is a surgeon.
speechPrompt: The book that you recommended was brilliant.

title: Lesson 135 — Indefinite Pronouns: Someone, Anybody, Nothing, Everyone
explanation: Indefinite pronouns refer to non-specific people or things. They take singular verbs ('Everyone is ready', NOT 'Everyone are ready').
exampleText: Example: Everyone is excited about the upcoming holiday.
speechPrompt: Does anybody know the correct answer?

title: Lesson 136 — Demonstrative Pronouns: This, That, These, Those
explanation: Use 'this/these' for things near in time/space, and 'that/those' for distant things. Ensure singular/plural agreement with following verbs.
exampleText: Example: These are my favorite pictures from the trip.
speechPrompt: That was a fantastic performance last night.

title: Lesson 137 — Reciprocal Pronouns: Each other vs One another
explanation: Use 'each other' typically for two subjects, and 'one another' for three or more. Both express mutual action.
exampleText: Example: The two rivals shook hands with each other.
speechPrompt: Team members supported one another throughout the project.

title: Lesson 138 — Dummy Subject Pronouns: 'It' and 'There'
explanation: Use 'it' for weather, time, distance, and identification ('It is raining'). Use 'there' to state existence ('There are three reasons').
exampleText: Example: It is starting to rain heavily outside.
speechPrompt: There is a solution to every challenge.

title: Lesson 139 — Common Pronoun Mistakes in Spoken Sentences
explanation: Avoid saying 'Me and John went' (correct: 'John and I went') or 'Between you and I' (correct: 'Between you and me').
exampleText: Example: John and I completed the report on time.
speechPrompt: This secret stays between you and me.

title: Lesson 140 — Gerunds vs Infinitives: Enjoy swimming vs Want to swim
explanation: Some verbs take a gerund (-ing) as an object (enjoy, avoid, suggest, consider). Other verbs take an infinitive (want, decide, hope, plan).
exampleText: Example: I enjoy reading fiction in my free time.
speechPrompt: She decided to study medicine at university.

title: Lesson 141 — Verbs Changing Meaning with Gerund or Infinitive
explanation: Verbs like 'stop', 'remember', and 'forget' change meaning: 'stop to smoke' (pause in order to smoke) vs 'stop smoking' (quit the habit).
exampleText: Example: I remember meeting him at the conference last year.
speechPrompt: Don't forget to lock the door when you leave.

title: Lesson 142 — Adjectives Ending in '-ed' vs '-ing'
explanation: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels ('I am bored'). -ing adjectives describe the thing/situation causing the feeling ('The class is boring').
exampleText: Example: I was fascinating by the story because the plot was interesting.
speechPrompt: She was bored during the long lecture.

title: Lesson 147 — Indefinite Articles 'A' & 'An' Phonetic Rules
explanation: Use 'a' before consonant sounds ('a university', 'a European') and 'an' before vowel sounds ('an hour', 'an honest person'). Base choice on sound, not spelling.
exampleText: Example: He is an honest man who works at a university.
speechPrompt: It took an hour to arrive at the station.

title: Lesson 148 — Definite Article 'The' Essential Guidelines
explanation: Use 'the' when referring to specific items known to speaker and listener, unique things (the sun, the world), or superlatives (the best).
exampleText: Example: The sun sets in the west.
speechPrompt: Could you pass me the salt on the table?

title: Lesson 149 — Zero Article: When NOT to Use Articles
explanation: Do NOT use articles before general plural nouns, uncountable abstract concepts, names of languages, academic subjects, or meals.
exampleText: Example: Knowledge is power.
speechPrompt: She is fluent in English and French.

title: Lesson 150 — Quantifiers: 'Some' vs 'Any' Rules
explanation: Use 'some' in positive affirmative sentences and polite offers/requests ('Would you like some tea?'). Use 'any' in negative sentences and general questions.
exampleText: Example: Do you have any questions regarding the lesson?
speechPrompt: I bought some fresh apples at the market.

title: Lesson 151 — Quantifiers: 'Much', 'Many', & 'A Lot Of'
explanation: Use 'many' with countable nouns, 'much' with uncountable nouns (mostly in questions/negatives), and 'a lot of' with both in affirmative statements.
exampleText: Example: There aren't many places left in the hall.
speechPrompt: How much time do we have before departure?

title: Lesson 152 — Quantifiers: 'Few' vs 'A Few' & 'Little' vs 'A Little'
explanation: 'A few' (countable) and 'a little' (uncountable) mean 'a small positive amount'. 'Few' and 'little' without 'a' have negative connotations meaning 'almost none'.
exampleText: Example: I have a few friends in the city who can help us.
speechPrompt: There is little water left in the jug.

title: Lesson 153 — Determiners: 'Each' vs 'Every'
explanation: 'Each' considers items individually (usually two or more). 'Every' considers items collectively as a group (three or more). Both take singular verbs.
exampleText: Example: Each student received an individual certificate.
speechPrompt: Every employee must attend the quarterly meeting.

title: Lesson 154 — Determiners: 'Both', 'Either', & 'Neither'
explanation: Use 'both' for two items together (plural verb). Use 'either' (one or the other) and 'neither' (not one nor the other) with singular verbs.
exampleText: Example: Neither of the two candidates was selected.
speechPrompt: Both of my brothers live in Sydney.

title: Lesson 155 — Determiners: 'All', 'Most', 'Whole', & 'No'
explanation: Use 'all' with plural/uncountable nouns, 'whole' with singular countable nouns ('the whole day'), and 'no' before nouns to express zero quantity.
exampleText: Example: I spent the whole day preparing for the exam.
speechPrompt: All students must submit their work today.

title: Lesson 156 — Articles with Geographical Names & Places
explanation: Use 'the' with oceans, rivers, mountain ranges, desert regions, and plural country names (the USA, the Netherlands). Omit articles for single mountains, lakes, or most countries.
exampleText: Example: We sailed across the Mediterranean Sea.
speechPrompt: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.

title: Lesson 157 — Mastering Articles & Quantifiers in Fast Speech
explanation: Proper article usage prevents unnatural pauses and makes your spoken English sound effortless and grammatically sound.
exampleText: Example: She gave me a piece of useful advice.
speechPrompt: I need a few more minutes to complete this.

title: Lesson 158 — Capitalization Rules in Written English
explanation: Capitalize proper nouns, days of the week, months, holidays, titles, national adjectives, and the first word of every sentence.
exampleText: Example: We will visit Paris in July with Professor Smith.
speechPrompt: English and Spanish are widely spoken.

title: Lesson 159 — Comma Rules: Separating Clauses & Lists
explanation: Use commas to separate items in a series, after introductory clauses, and before coordinating conjunctions connecting independent clauses.
exampleText: Example: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
speechPrompt: I bought apples, bananas, and oranges.

title: Lesson 160 — Apostrophe Rules: Possessives vs Contractions
explanation: Use apostrophes for contractions (it's = it is) and possessives (dog's bone). Plural possessives place the apostrophe after the 's' (teachers' lounge).
exampleText: Example: The children's playground was recently renovated.
speechPrompt: It's important to double-check your work.

title: Lesson 161 — Quotation Marks & Direct Speech Formatting
explanation: Enclose exact spoken words in quotation marks. Place commas and periods inside quotation marks in standard American formatting.
exampleText: Example: She said, "I will arrive at six o'clock."
speechPrompt: "We are ready," declared the team lead.

title: Lesson 162 — Semicolons & Colons Usage Masterclass
explanation: Use a semicolon to join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction. Use a colon to introduce a list, explanation, or quote.
exampleText: Example: I have a big deadline tomorrow; therefore, I must stay up late.
speechPrompt: Please bring three items: a pen, a notebook, and a ruler.

title: Lesson 163 — Hyphens & Dashes: Rules & Differences
explanation: Use hyphens to connect compound adjectives before nouns ('a well-known author'). Use em-dashes (—) to emphasize or set off parenthetical thoughts.
exampleText: Example: She is a well-known scientist in her field.
speechPrompt: This is a fast-growing tech company.

title: Lesson 164 — Question Marks & Exclamation Marks Tone Control
explanation: Use question marks only for direct questions (not indirect ones). Use exclamation marks sparingly to convey strong emotion or urgent commands.
exampleText: Example: Where are you heading right now?
speechPrompt: What a wonderful surprise this is!

title: Lesson 165 — Parentheses & Brackets in Professional Text
explanation: Use parentheses () to add supplementary or non-essential commentary. Use square brackets [] for editorial clarifications within quotes.
exampleText: Example: The event (which was held outdoors) was a great success.
speechPrompt: The report includes all recent figures.
