title: Lesson 166 — Common Punctuation Traps in Written Communication
explanation: Avoid comma splices (joining two independent sentences with only a comma). Use a semicolon or conjunction instead.
exampleText: Example: I was hungry; however, I waited for my friend.
speechPrompt: She loves reading; she reads every night.

title: Lesson 167 — Punctuation Pause Cues for Spoken Intonation
explanation: Punctuation marks act as visual roadmap cues for natural speech pauses, breath management, and pitch changes.
exampleText: Example: When the bell rang, everyone stood up immediately.
speechPrompt: In summary, we achieved all our goals.

title: Lesson 168 — Active vs Passive Voice Structural Comparison
explanation: Active voice focuses on the performer of the action (Subject + Verb + Object). Passive voice focuses on the recipient of the action (Object + Be + Past Participle).
exampleText: Example: The chef prepared a exquisite dinner.
speechPrompt: An exquisite dinner was prepared by the chef.

title: Lesson 169 — Converting Present & Past Tenses to Passive
explanation: Simple Present Passive: am/is/are + V3 ('Letters are delivered daily'). Simple Past Passive: was/were + V3 ('The house was built in 1990').
exampleText: Example: The new bridge was opened by the mayor yesterday.
speechPrompt: Spanish is spoken in many countries.

title: Lesson 170 — Passive Voice with Modal Verbs (Can Be Done, Should Be Sent)
explanation: Form passive modals using Modal + Be + Past Participle (e.g., 'The document must be signed before Friday').
exampleText: Example: All applications must be submitted by midnight.
speechPrompt: This problem can be easily solved.
optionsString: must be submitted,must submit,must submitting,must have submit

title: Lesson 171 — Strategic Uses of Passive Voice in Formal & Technical English
explanation: Use passive voice when the agent is unknown, obvious, or less important than the action itself, or in formal academic/business reports.
exampleText: Example: The experiment was conducted under controlled laboratory conditions.
speechPrompt: Our server was updated last night.

title: Lesson 172 — Understanding Phrasal Verbs & Separable Rules
explanation: Phrasal verbs consist of a verb + particle (preposition or adverb). Separable phrasal verbs allow objects between verb and particle ('turn it on'). Pronouns MUST go in between.
exampleText: Example: Please turn the lights off before leaving.
speechPrompt: Could you turn it on?
optionsString: turn off,turn off it,turn it off,turning off

title: Lesson 173 — Essential Phrasal Verbs with 'Get'
explanation: Master common 'get' phrasal verbs: get along with (have a good relationship), get over (recover from), get by (survive financially).
exampleText: Example: She gets along very well with all her colleagues.
speechPrompt: It took him a month to get over the flu.

title: Lesson 174 — Essential Phrasal Verbs with 'Take'
explanation: Master 'take' phrasal verbs: take off (depart / remove), take over (assume control), take after (resemble a family member).
exampleText: Example: The plane will take off in ten minutes.
speechPrompt: He takes after his father in demeanor.

title: Lesson 175 — Essential Phrasal Verbs with 'Turn'
explanation: Master 'turn' phrasal verbs: turn down (refuse / lower volume), turn up (appear / increase volume), turn out (result in).
exampleText: Example: She turned down the job offer because of the location.
speechPrompt: He surprisingly turned up at the party late.

title: Lesson 176 — Essential Phrasal Verbs with 'Look'
explanation: Master 'look' phrasal verbs: look after (care for), look forward to (anticipate eagerly + gerund), look up (search for information).
exampleText: Example: I am really looking forward to visiting you next week.
speechPrompt: She looks after her younger brother.
optionsString: looking forward to,looking after,looking up,looking into

title: Lesson 177 — Essential Phrasal Verbs with 'Bring' & 'Give'
explanation: Master: bring up (mention / raise a child), give up (stop trying / quit habit), give away (donate / reveal a secret).
exampleText: Example: Don't give up on your dreams.
speechPrompt: She brought up an interesting point during the meeting.

title: Lesson 178 — Essential Phrasal Verbs with 'Come' & 'Go'
explanation: Master: come across (find unexpectedly), come up with (invent/suggest an idea), go on (continue), go through (experience/examine).
exampleText: Example: She came across an old photograph in the drawer.
speechPrompt: He came up with a brilliant business idea.
optionsString: came across,came up with,went on,went through

title: Lesson 179 — Essential Phrasal Verbs with 'Put'
explanation: Master: put off (postpone), put up with (tolerate), put on (wear / organize), put away (store in proper place).
exampleText: Example: Never put off until tomorrow what you can do today.
speechPrompt: I cannot put up with this loud noise any longer.
optionsString: put off,put up with,put on,put away

title: Lesson 180 — Essential Phrasal Verbs with 'Call' & 'Break'
explanation: Master: call off (cancel), call back (return phone call), break down (stop functioning / become emotional), break out (start suddenly).
exampleText: Example: The outdoor match was called off due to heavy rain.
speechPrompt: My car broke down on the highway this morning.

title: Lesson 181 — Business & Workplace Phrasal Verbs
explanation: Master professional phrasal verbs: carry out (execute a plan), follow up on (check status), set up (arrange a meeting), wind up (conclude).
exampleText: Example: We need to set up a conference call for tomorrow.
speechPrompt: Our team will carry out the project plan successfully.

title: Lesson 182 — Three-Word Phrasal Verbs (Run out of, Catch up with)
explanation: Three-word phrasal verbs are inseparable: run out of (deplete supply), catch up with (reach the same level), cut down on (reduce consumption).
exampleText: Example: We have run out of printer paper.
speechPrompt: I need to catch up with my old friends.
optionsString: run out of,catch up with,cut down on,look up to

title: Lesson 183 — Phrasal Verbs for Travel, Socializing & Daily Life
explanation: Master travel phrasal verbs: check in (register at hotel/airport), drop off (deliver someone), pick up (collect someone), see off (say goodbye at departure).
exampleText: Example: My friend dropped me off at the airport terminal.
speechPrompt: We checked in at the hotel reception.

title: Lesson 184 — Using Phrasal Verbs Naturally in Everyday Speech
explanation: Using appropriate phrasal verbs makes your English sound conversational, warm, and natural rather than overly rigid.
exampleText: Example: Let's catch up over lunch this afternoon.
speechPrompt: Hold on a minute while I grab my coat.

title: Lesson 185 — Prefixes & Suffixes: Rapid Vocabulary Expansion
explanation: Prefixes (un-, dis-, re-, im-, mis-) change meaning. Suffixes (-ment, -tion, -able, -ful, -less) change word class (e.g., happy -> happiness).
exampleText: Example: Her act of kindness brought great happiness to everyone.
speechPrompt: It is impossible to finish this without assistance.

title: Lesson 186 — Sentence Types: Simple, Compound & Complex Structures
explanation: Simple sentences have one independent clause. Compound sentences join clauses with FANBOYS. Complex sentences use subordinating conjunctions.
exampleText: Example: Although she was tired, she completed the report and sent it to her boss.
speechPrompt: He likes tea, but she prefers coffee.

title: Lesson 187 — Word Order Rules: Subject-Verb-Object-Manner-Place-Time
explanation: English standard word order follows SVOMPT (Subject + Verb + Object + Manner + Place + Time). E.g., 'He played tennis brilliantly at the park yesterday'.
exampleText: Example: She played the piano beautifully at the concert last night.
speechPrompt: They drove carefully on the highway during the storm.
optionsString: played the piano beautifully,played beautifully the piano,beautifully played the piano,the piano played beautifully

title: Lesson 188 — Direct vs Reported Speech (Backshifting Tenses)
explanation: When reporting past speech, shift tenses back one step (Present Simple -> Past Simple; Present Continuous -> Past Continuous; Will -> Would).
exampleText: Example: She said that she was working on a new project.
speechPrompt: He told us that he would call us back later.

title: Lesson 189 — Inversion for Strong Emphasis in Formal Speech
explanation: Place negative adverbs (Never, Seldom, Rarely, Hardly) at the start of a sentence followed by auxiliary inversion ('Never have I seen such beauty').
exampleText: Example: Rarely have I heard such an inspiring presentation.
speechPrompt: Never will I forget this extraordinary trip.
optionsString: Rarely have I heard,Rarely I have heard,Rarely heard I,Rarely I heard

title: Lesson 190 — Formal vs Informal Writing Styles & Email Etiquette
explanation: Use formal language (no contractions, precise vocabulary, polite salutations) in business emails, and informal contractions in casual messages.
exampleText: Example: Dear Sir/Madam, I am writing to inquire about the position.
speechPrompt: I look forward to hearing from you soon.

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 191 — Adverbs of Manner, Degree & Frequency
explanation: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, seldom) go before main verbs but after 'be'.
exampleText: Example: She always arrives at the office early.
speechPrompt: He spoke clearly and persuasively during the speech.
optionsString: always arrives,arrives always,is always arriving,always arrive

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 192 — Intensifiers: Very, Really, Extremely, Quite, Fairly
explanation: Intensifiers modify the strength of adjectives. Extreme adjectives (fantastic, exhausted, freezing) take 'absolutely' rather than 'very'.
exampleText: Example: I was absolutely exhausted after the marathon.
speechPrompt: The movie was extremely interesting.

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 193 — Filler Words & Soft Hesitation in Natural Speech
explanation: Native speakers use natural fillers (well, actually, you know, I mean, as a matter of fact) to gain thinking time without breaking conversation flow.
exampleText: Example: Well, to be honest, I haven't considered that option yet.
speechPrompt: Actually, that makes a lot of sense.

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 194 — Opinion Softeners: Politely Expressing Views
explanation: Soften firm statements using phrases like 'In my opinion', 'It seems to me', 'From my perspective', or 'I would suggest'.
exampleText: Example: In my opinion, we should focus on quality rather than speed.
speechPrompt: It seems to me that we need more data.
optionsString: In my opinion,It seems to me,From my view,I think

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 195 — Expressing Agreement & Disagreement Gracefully
explanation: Agree enthusiastically ('I completely agree', 'You're absolutely right'). Disagree politely ('I see your point, but...', 'I'm afraid I have a slightly different view').
exampleText: Example: I see your point, but we must also consider the budget.
speechPrompt: I couldn't agree with you more.
optionsString: I see your point but,I completely agree,You are wrong,I disagree

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 196 — Clarification Strategies in Live Conversations
explanation: Ask for clarification politely: 'Could you rephrase that?', 'If I understand correctly, you mean...', 'Could you elaborate on that point?'
exampleText: Example: Could you please elaborate on that last point?
speechPrompt: If I understand correctly, you want us to start today.

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 197 — Sentence Stress & Rhythm in Spoken English
explanation: English is a stress-timed language. Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) are stressed, while structure words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries) are unstressed.
exampleText: Example: We NEED to FOCUS on the MAIN OBJECTIVES.
speechPrompt: She WANTS to BUY a NEW CAR.
optionsString: NEED focus MAIN OBJECTIVES,We need to focus,on the main objectives,focus on main

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 198 — Intonation Patterns: Rising vs Falling Tones
explanation: Use falling intonation for statements and Wh- questions. Use rising intonation for Yes/No questions and checking understanding.
exampleText: Example: Are you coming with us tonight? (Rising)
speechPrompt: Where do you live? (Falling)

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 199 — Connected Speech: Linking Consonant to Vowel Sounds
explanation: When a word ends in a consonant and the next starts with a vowel, link them smoothly (e.g., 'an apple' sounds like 'a-napple'; 'check it out' sounds like 'che-ki-tout').
exampleText: Example: Can you check it out for me?
speechPrompt: He held an apple in his hand.

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 200 — Connected Speech: Elision & Blending Sounds
explanation: In fast natural speech, sounds drop or blend ('next door' -> 'nexdoor'; 'must be' -> 'musbe'; 'going to' -> 'gonna').
exampleText: Example: He must be arriving any minute now.
speechPrompt: They are going to launch the product tomorrow.

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 201 — Expanding Academic & Business Vocabulary
explanation: Replace weak words with precise formal alternatives: 'big' -> 'substantial'; 'change' -> 'modify'; 'help' -> 'assist'; 'show' -> 'demonstrate'.
exampleText: Example: The team demonstrated a substantial improvement in performance.
speechPrompt: We need to modify our marketing strategy.

category: Fluency & Vocabulary Building (Adverbs, Intensifiers & Speaking Tips)
title: Lesson 202 — Mastering Idiomatic Expressions for Everyday Fluency
explanation: Idioms add color to speech. Examples: 'hit the nail on the head' (be exactly right), 'piece of cake' (very easy), 'break the ice' (initiate conversation).
exampleText: Example: His explanation hit the nail on the head.
speechPrompt: The exam turned out to be a piece of cake.
optionsString: hit the nail on the head,piece of cake,break the ice,under the weather
correctOption: hit the nail on the head

title: Lesson 203 — Adjective Order Rules (OSASCOMP Formula)
explanation: When using multiple adjectives before a noun, follow OSASCOMP: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Color, Origin, Material, Purpose (e.g., 'a beautiful small old round wooden table').
exampleText: Example: She wore an elegant long red silk dress to the gala.
speechPrompt: He bought a charming antique Italian leather jacket.
optionsString: elegant long red silk,red long elegant silk,silk red long elegant,long red silk elegant

title: Lesson 204 — Comparative & Superlative Adjectives Rules
explanation: Short adjectives take -er/-est ('faster', 'fastest'). Long adjectives take more/most ('more beautiful'). Irregulars: good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, far/further/furthest.
exampleText: Example: This is the most challenging project I have ever undertaken.
speechPrompt: She is much taller than her sister.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 205 — Subject-Verb Agreement: Singular & Plural Harmony
explanation: Ensure singular subjects take singular verbs and plural subjects take plural verbs, even when long prepositional phrases separate them.
exampleText: Example: The box of colorful crayons is sitting on the desk.
speechPrompt: The students in the classroom are listening attentively.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 206 — Subject-Verb Agreement with Collective Nouns
explanation: Collective nouns (team, committee, family, jury) take singular verbs in American English when acting as a unified unit ('The committee has reached a consensus').
exampleText: Example: The committee has announced its final decision.
speechPrompt: My family is planning a summer vacation.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 207 — Avoiding Double Negatives in Spoken English
explanation: Double negatives ('I don't know nothing') are grammatically incorrect in standard English. Express negative ideas with a single negative word ('I don't know anything').
exampleText: Example: I don't know anything about that issue.
speechPrompt: She didn't see anybody at the park.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 208 — Correct Pronoun Alignment in Complex Contexts
explanation: Match pronouns in gender and number with their antecedents. E.g., 'Every student must submit their (or his/her) project on time'.
exampleText: Example: Every employee should double-check their schedule.
speechPrompt: Each member brought her own equipment.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 209 — Dangling & Misplaced Modifiers and How to Fix Them
explanation: Modifiers must clearly attach to the noun they describe. Avoid dangling modifiers ('Walking down the street, the trees were pretty' -> 'Walking down the street, I saw pretty trees').
exampleText: Example: Walking down the street, I noticed a new coffee shop.
speechPrompt: Having finished the report, she turned off her computer.
optionsString: Walking down the street I noticed,Walking down the street the shop noticed,Walking the street noticed I,Noticed walking street
correctOption: Walking down the street I noticed

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 210 — Parallel Structure in Lists & Sentences
explanation: Maintain consistent grammatical forms when listing items or connecting ideas with conjunctions (e.g., 'He likes swimming, running, and cycling', NOT 'and to cycle').
exampleText: Example: She enjoys swimming, hiking, and reading historical novels.
speechPrompt: He promised to study hard, practice daily, and attend all lectures.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 211 — Avoiding Redundancy & Wordy Expressions
explanation: Eliminate redundant phrasing in professional communication: 'repeat again' -> 'repeat'; 'close proximity' -> 'close'; 'added bonus' -> 'bonus'.
exampleText: Example: Please repeat the instructions clearly.
speechPrompt: The office is in close proximity to the station.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 212 — Preposition Mistakes to Eliminate in Conversation
explanation: Common errors: 'discuss about' (wrong -> 'discuss'), 'married with' (wrong -> 'married to'), 'listen music' (wrong -> 'listen to music').
exampleText: Example: She has been married to my uncle for twenty years.
speechPrompt: Let's listen to some relaxing music.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 213 — Tense Consistency Across Paragraphs & Narratives
explanation: Do not shift abruptly between past and present tenses without a logical reason when telling a story or describing a process.
exampleText: Example: He walked into the room, sat down on the chair, and opened his book.
speechPrompt: When she arrived, everyone welcomed her warmly.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 214 — Common Grammar Traps in Job Interviews
explanation: Use strong past tense action verbs for achievements ('managed', 'implemented', 'orchestrated') and avoid overly tentative language.
exampleText: Example: I successfully managed a team of ten software developers.
speechPrompt: She spearheaded the new marketing campaign.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 215 — Spoken vs Written English Grammar Conventions
explanation: Recognize when informal contractions and reduced forms are acceptable (spoken/casual text) versus when full forms are required (formal writing).
exampleText: Example: We are writing to confirm your reservation details.
speechPrompt: I'm gonna leave soon.

category: General Grammar Rules, Common Mistakes & Quizzes
title: Lesson 216 — Comprehensive Grammar Diagnostic Checkup
explanation: Test your overall accuracy across modal verbs, tenses, prepositions, articles, and sentence structure.

title: Lesson 217 — Final Grammar Mastery Review & Assessment
explanation: Consolidate all 234 grammar rules and speaking drills to ensure natural confidence, clear pronunciation, and high structural accuracy.

speechPrompt: I am confident in my ability to speak English clearly.

title: Lesson 218 — Idioms for Emotions: Happiness, Anger & Stress
explanation: Learn expressive idioms: 'on cloud nine' (ecstatically happy), 'see red' (become furious), 'under the weather' (slightly unwell), 'over the moon' (delighted).
exampleText: Example: She was on cloud nine when she received the promotion.
speechPrompt: I am feeling a bit under the weather today.
optionsString: on cloud nine,under the weather,seeing red,over the moon

title: Lesson 219 — Idioms for Work, Success & Perseverance
explanation: Learn workplace idioms: 'hit the ground running' (start with immediate energy), 'learn the ropes' (master new tasks), 'burn the midnight oil' (work late into night).
exampleText: Example: It took me a few weeks to learn the ropes at my new job.
speechPrompt: We had to burn the midnight oil to meet the deadline.
optionsString: learn the ropes,burn the midnight oil,hit the ground running,cut corners

title: Lesson 220 — Idioms for Money, Decisions & Opportunities
explanation: Learn decision idioms: 'at a crossroads' (facing a big choice), 'break the bank' (cost too much), 'bite the bullet' (face a tough situation bravely).
exampleText: Example: We decided to bite the bullet and invest in new equipment.
speechPrompt: This vacation won't break the bank.
optionsString: bite the bullet,break the bank,at a crossroads,cost an arm and a leg

title: Lesson 221 — Descriptive Adjectives for Character & Personality
explanation: Expand personality vocabulary: meticulous (paying great attention to detail), charismatic (inspiring charm), compassionate (kind/empathetic), reliable (trustworthy).
exampleText: Example: Our team lead is exceptionally meticulous in her work.
speechPrompt: He is a compassionate and reliable friend.

title: Lesson 222 — Descriptive Vocabulary for Atmosphere & Settings
explanation: Describe places vividly: tranquil (peaceful/calm), bustling (full of noisy activity), picturesque (charming like a picture), vibrant (energetic/colorful).
exampleText: Example: We spent the weekend in a tranquil mountain village.
speechPrompt: The bustling city market was filled with vivid colors.

title: Lesson 223 — Strong Verbs vs Weak Verbs with 'Very'
explanation: Upgrade your vocabulary by replacing 'very + weak verb/adjective': 'very tired' -> 'exhausted'; 'very clean' -> 'spotless'; 'very cold' -> 'freezing'; 'very smart' -> 'brilliant'.
exampleText: Example: After the long hike, we were completely exhausted.
speechPrompt: The kitchen was sparkling and spotless.

title: Lesson 224 — Collocations with 'Take', 'Have', & 'Make'
explanation: Natural verb-noun pairings: take a break, take a risk, have a conversation, have an impact, make progress, make an effort.
exampleText: Example: We made significant progress during today's brainstorming session.
speechPrompt: Let's take a quick fifteen-minute break.

title: Lesson 225 — Collocations with 'Do', 'Pay', & 'Keep'
explanation: Natural verb-noun pairings: do business, do a favor, pay attention, pay a compliment, keep a promise, keep in mind.
exampleText: Example: Please keep in mind that the deadline is tomorrow.
speechPrompt: You should pay close attention to the instructions.
optionsString: keep in mind,pay attention,do a favor,keep a promise

title: Lesson 226 — Expressing Sympathy, Congratulations & Praise
explanation: Conversational phrases: 'I am so sorry for your loss', 'Warmest congratulations on your achievement!', 'Kudos to you for a job well done!'
exampleText: Example: Warmest congratulations on your remarkable promotion!
speechPrompt: I am so sorry to hear about your bad news.

title: Lesson 227 — Making Proposals, Suggestions & Recommendations
explanation: Use persuasive phrases: 'How about we try...?', 'I strongly recommend that we...', 'Why don't we consider...?', 'It might be beneficial to...'
exampleText: Example: I strongly recommend that we test the software thoroughly.
speechPrompt: How about we schedule the meeting for Tuesday morning?
optionsString: strongly recommend,how about,why don't we,I suggest

title: Lesson 228 — Summarizing & Paraphrasing Ideas in Speaking
explanation: Useful transition phrases: 'To sum up...', 'In short...', 'To put it another way...', 'In essence, what I am saying is...'
exampleText: Example: To sum up, our strategy focuses on quality and customer satisfaction.
speechPrompt: In short, we need to increase our efficiency.
optionsString: To sum up,In short,In essence,To put it another way

title: Lesson 229 — Storytelling Techniques & Narrative Connectors
explanation: Engage listeners with narrative markers: 'It all started when...', 'Out of nowhere...', 'To make a long story short...', 'Before I knew it...'
exampleText: Example: To make a long story short, we landed safely and enjoyed the trip.
speechPrompt: Out of nowhere, a heavy downpour started.
optionsString: To make a long story short,Out of nowhere,Before I knew it,It all started when
correctOption: To make a long story short

title: Lesson 230 — Countable vs Uncountable Nouns & Tricky Nouns
explanation: Uncountable nouns (information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment, news) never take 'a/an' and do not add '-s'. Use 'a piece of' to count them.
exampleText: Example: He gave me a valuable piece of advice.
speechPrompt: All the news was positive.

title: Lesson 231 — Plural Noun Rules & Irregular Plurals
explanation: Irregular plurals change vowels (man -> men, tooth -> teeth, mouse -> mice) or stay identical (sheep, deer, fish). Always-plural nouns take plural verbs (pants, scissors, glasses).
exampleText: Example: Where are my reading glasses?
speechPrompt: The sheep were grazing peacefully in the field.

title: Lesson 232 — Compound Nouns & Possessive Nouns Rules
explanation: Possessive 's is used for people and animals ('John's car'). Use 'of' for inanimate objects ('the roof of the house'). Compound nouns form plurals on the head noun ('passers-by').
exampleText: Example: The roof of the house was damaged in the storm.
speechPrompt: They are my brother's close friends.
optionsString: roof of the house,house's roof,roof house,roofs house

title: Lesson 233 — Causative Verbs: Make, Have, Get, Let, & Help
explanation: Structure rules: Make/Have/Let + object + base verb ('She made me clean'); Get + object + to-infinitive ('I got him to repair the sink'); Help takes base verb or to-infinitive.
exampleText: Example: She made me rewrite the entire essay.
speechPrompt: I will get the mechanic to check the brakes.
optionsString: made me rewrite,made me to rewrite,got me rewrite,let me to rewrite

title: Lesson 234 — Using 'Suggest' & 'Recommend' Correctly
explanation: Never say 'suggest me to do'. Correct structures: 'suggest + -ing' ('I suggest taking a break') OR 'suggest that + subject + base verb' ('I suggest that he take a break').
exampleText: Example: I suggest taking a short walk to clear your head.
speechPrompt: The doctor recommended that she rest for three days.
optionsString: taking,to take,that he takes,him to take
